tone_statements.citation: Singha, Y. Arunima. 2017. A Descriptive Grammar of Reang. Ph.D. thesis, Dept. of Linguistics, Assam University, Silchar. xxi+360 pp.
tone_statements.quote: 3.2. Tones Like other Tibeto-Burman languages, Reang is a tone language in which a change in the pitch of the syllable corresponds to a change in its meaning. Reang has two lexical tones namely high and low. (i) Low: the tension of the vocal cords in the production of a syllable is relatively low, causing a low pitch. The low tone is marked by the symbol / ˋ/. (ii) High: the tension of the vocal cords in the production of a syllable is relatively high, causing a high pitch. It is represented by the symbol / ʹ/. … ̸ kəˋtúŋ̸ „wool‟ ̸ kəˋtùŋ ̸ „hot‟ ̸ hór ̸ „fire‟ ̸ hòr ̸ „night‟ …
tone_statements.locator: ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.2 'Tones' with Table no 3 'Tones in Reang', pp. 24-25

tone_statements.citation: Singha, Y. Arunima & K. Kalpi Singha. 2017. Linguistic and Cultural Aspects of Reang. Language in India 17(7) (July 2017): 1-11. ISSN 1930-2940.
tone_statements.quote: 1.14. Typological Overview The various typological features found in Reang are: (i) Reang is a tonal language. It has two tones, high and low. (ii) Reang exhibits a six-vowel system found in most of the Tibeto-Burman languages and twenty consonantal phonemes.

sources.citation: Debbarma, Sheela. 2021. A comparative phonology of Kokborok dialects: an analytical study of literary Kokborok, Reang and Jamatia dialects. Ph.D. thesis, Dept. of English, Tripura University (guide Chaitali Gorai). 230 pp. Shodhganga hdl 10603/368085.
sources.note: No Reang word-stress rule. 4.2.5 Syllable structure in Reang (pp.139-51); 4.3.4 Tones in Reang Dialect (pp.166-67): three tones (rising, falling, level) distinguish homophones, e.g. /lai/ leaf (rising) / easy (falling) / to cross (level); sesquisyllabic prefixes retain tone. Only generic remark p.157 that 'stress or accent is also associated with tone.. in stress languages such as English'.

tone.says: Two lexical tones, high and low, marked with acute and grave; a change in the pitch of a syllable changes meaning (e.g. hór 'fire' vs hòr 'night'). Nothing is said about word stress.

sources.citation: Reang, G. K. 2007. Kaw Bru Abhidhan [Kau Bru dictionary, in Bengali]. Agartala: Tribal Research and Cultural Institute, Govt. of Tripura.
sources.note: Front-matter 'rules of Kaubru pronunciation' (Bengali): Kokborok and Kaubru are basically one language differing slightly in pronunciation; a dot over a letter marks raised pitch that changes meaning (tone). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Gan Chaudhury, Jagadish. 1983. The Reangs of Tripura. Agartala: Tribal Research Institute, Govt. of Tripura.
sources.note: Sec. 6 Language pp.11-12: twelve grammatical observations; no. 12: 'The same word pronounced in low voice bears one meaning, while pronounced in high tone indicates a different meaning.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Singha, Y. Arunima & K. Kalpi Singha. 2017. Linguistic and Cultural Aspects of Reang. Language in India 17(7) (July 2017): 1-11. ISSN 1930-2940.
sources.quote: 1.14. Typological Overview The various typological features found in Reang are: (i) Reang is a tonal language. It has two tones, high and low. (ii) Reang exhibits a six-vowel system found in most of the Tibeto-Burman languages and twenty consonantal phonemes.
sources.note: Typological overview states Reang is a tonal language with two tones, high and low (alongside 6 vowels and 20 consonants); no further tonal analysis, no minimal pairs in this article; nothing on stress. Consistent with the two-tone (high/low) analysis in Singha's 2017 thesis and Reang 2019, against Debbarma 2021's three tones.
